name: Software Architect Roadmap
tagline: From structuring one codebase to choosing, justifying and evolving whole systems
summary: Architecture is the set of decisions that are expensive to reverse, so this path is about earning the judgement to make them. It starts where every architect starts — building things — then moves through the structural patterns that keep one codebase changeable, the data guarantees that constrain every design, the distributed-systems reality that appears the moment there is a second machine, the integration patterns that connect services, and finally how systems are evolved and how decisions are recorded and measured.

steps.label: Programming fundamentals
steps.note: An architect who cannot still read and write the code loses the feedback loop that keeps designs honest, so this never stops being step one.

steps.label: Build and run real services
steps.note: Judgement about designs comes from having operated a few; you need the memory of a bad decision costing you a weekend before the patterns mean anything.

steps.label: HTTP & API design
steps.note: Nearly every boundary you will draw is exposed over HTTP, and the contract at that boundary outlives the code behind it.

steps.label: Databases
steps.note: Data outlives services: the storage choice and the schema are the hardest parts of any system to change later, so they anchor the whole design.

steps.label: Layered architecture
steps.note: Start with the simplest structural idea — separate presentation, logic and data access — and learn precisely where it starts to leak.

steps.label: Clean & hexagonal architecture
steps.note: Inverting dependencies so business rules do not import the database or the framework is what makes a codebase testable and portable across a decade of tooling changes.

steps.label: Domain-driven design
steps.note: Bounded contexts and a shared language are how you decide where the seams belong; almost every bad service split is really a missing domain model.

steps.label: Modular monolith
steps.note: Enforcing module boundaries inside one deployable gives you most of the benefit of services with none of the network, and it is the correct default for most teams.

steps.label: Transactions & isolation
steps.note: Knowing exactly what a transaction promises — and what isolation level your database actually runs — determines whether a design needs distributed coordination at all.

steps.label: Replication & sharding
steps.note: How data is copied and split decides your read scaling, your failure modes and which queries become impossible, so it belongs in the design and not in a later migration.

steps.label: CAP theorem & consistency models
steps.note: This is the vocabulary for saying what a system gives up during a partition; without it 'highly available and strongly consistent' sounds like a requirement rather than a contradiction.

steps.label: Distributed systems
steps.note: Partial failure, timeouts, retries and clock skew are not edge cases but the normal operating condition of anything with two machines in it.

steps.label: Microservices & service boundaries
steps.note: Once you know both the modular alternative and the distributed cost, you can judge when independent deployment and scaling actually justify the network between components.

steps.label: Message queues & asynchrony
steps.note: Asynchronous messaging is the main tool for decoupling services in time, and it trades immediate consistency for availability — a trade an architect must make deliberately.

steps.label: Event-driven architecture
steps.note: Publishing facts instead of calling commands changes who depends on whom; it enables independent evolution and makes debugging and ordering much harder.

steps.label: Saga & distributed transactions
steps.note: When a business process spans services there is no single transaction, so you need compensation, idempotency and a clear story about intermediate states.

steps.label: API versioning & contracts
steps.note: Every boundary you create must be changeable without a coordinated release, and versioning discipline is what makes independent deployment real rather than nominal.

steps.label: Strangler fig & legacy migration
steps.note: Most architecture work is changing a running system, and incremental replacement behind a facade is the only approach that keeps the business alive during the rewrite.

steps.label: SLOs & quality attributes
steps.note: Latency, availability and durability targets turn vague non-functional requirements into numbers a design can be evaluated against.

steps.label: Observability
steps.note: A design you cannot observe cannot be verified or debugged, so tracing, metrics and log structure are architectural concerns and not an afterthought for the ops team.

steps.label: Architecture decision records
steps.note: Writing down the options, the choice and the consequences is what makes architecture reviewable, teachable and reversible when the context changes.

steps.label: Practise whole-system design
steps.note: Finish by walking a system from one server to a scaled-out design, naming the trade-off at each step — the exercise every topic above exists to support.
